core.big_idea: Law and tabernacle define rescued Israel's covenant vocation and the problem of holy presence among sinners.

passages.reading_note: Trace prior rescue, covenant vocation, conditional response, and holiness.
Track rescue preface, commands, divine manifestation, fear, and mediation.
Connect sanctuary purpose with the glory filling and governing Israel’s journey.
Use in Extended profile for New Covenant and sanctuary development.

core.metanarrative_position: Covenant and presence: the rescued nation receives vocation and law, while boundaries and tabernacle make visible the tension of a holy God dwelling among sinful people.
core.biblical_genre: Covenant narrative, law, sanctuary instruction, and apostolic interpretation

claims.statement: Exodus 19 grounds the covenant invitation in God’s prior rescue of Israel from Egypt.
Israel is called to covenant obedience and a vocation as treasured possession, kingdom of priests, and holy nation.
The Decalogue begins with the identity of the Lord who brought Israel out of slavery before stating covenant commands.
Sinai includes boundaries, divine manifestation, fear, and mediated speech, displaying the seriousness of holy presence.
The tabernacle is constructed so that God may dwell among Israel, and the filling glory both confirms presence and creates access limits.
Hebrews interprets the old covenant sanctuary and priestly system as limited and anticipatory in relation to Christ and the New Covenant.
The common moral, civil, and ceremonial division can be a later teaching tool, but Exodus does not present its laws under those three explicit labels.
claims.credible_alternative: Christian traditions differ over how useful the threefold category is and how continuity with Mosaic law should be described.
claims.interpretive_hinge: Whether a later systematic classification accurately clarifies or oversimplifies the covenant text.
claims.prohibited_overstatement: Do not call the threefold division an explicit biblical table of contents or use it to bypass contextual exegesis.

core.interpretation_skill: Read law and sanctuary within rescue and covenant narrative; test continuity claims through New Covenant texts rather than isolated transfer.

learning.foundation_objective: Explain how rescue, covenant vocation, law, boundaries, and tabernacle presence fit together at Sinai.
learning.extension_objective: Evaluate law-continuity models, use Hebrews responsibly, and distinguish the biblical covenant structure from later systematic categories.
know: Israel receives a priestly and holy vocation.
The tabernacle is built for divine presence among the people.
Hebrews develops the sanctuary theme around Christ.
understand: Holy presence is gift and danger in a sinful community.
Law must be read as covenant text before being applied across covenants.
practise: Classify a law claim by original context, canonical development, and present application.
become: A student who treats holiness seriously, obeys from gratitude, and refuses simplistic law transfer.
success_evidence: The student completes the Rescue-to-Presence map.
The student explains why Exodus 20:2 matters.
The student identifies the limits of the moral-civil-ceremonial classification.

zero_prep_card.objective: Students connect rescue, covenant vocation, law, and tabernacle presence and explain the problem of holy presence among sinners.
zero_prep_card.opening: Ask: What changes when a powerful and good king chooses to live among a community that is not yet trustworthy?
say: Sinai begins with rescue already accomplished.
Israel receives a vocation and covenant commands.
Boundaries and fear show the seriousness of God’s holiness.
The tabernacle expresses God’s desire to dwell among the people while access remains ordered and mediated.
ask: What comes before the covenant demands?
How does the tabernacle hold presence and access limits together?
zero_prep_card.do: Complete the Rescue, Vocation, Boundary, Presence map.
zero_prep_card.close: Pray for reverence, gratitude, obedience, and confidence in God’s completed work in Christ.

preparation.passage_context: Sinai follows the Exodus and wilderness provision. Exodus 19-24 establishes covenant; Exodus 25-40 develops sanctuary, priesthood, failure, renewal, construction, and filling glory. Hebrews later interprets the covenant and sanctuary through Christ.
text_observations: Exodus 19 explicitly moves from rescue to vocation and response.
Exodus 20 combines ethical commands with manifestation and mediated hearing.
Exodus 25 states the sanctuary purpose; Exodus 40 records glory filling and cloud guidance.
Moses cannot enter when the glory fills the tabernacle, showing presence and access tension.
interpretation_notes: Do not describe the Mosaic law merely as a failed attempt to earn salvation; it is covenant instruction for a rescued nation.
Do not transfer every stipulation directly to the church or dismiss it as useless.
Use Hebrews to follow inspired canonical development, not to mock or denigrate Judaism.
theological_guardrails: Do not use holiness language to shame bodies, disability, ethnicity, or ordinary human limitation.
Do not equate fear of God with panic induced by a controlling teacher or leader.
Do not claim the moral-civil-ceremonial division is explicit in Exodus.

likely_questions.question: Why could Moses not enter when the glory filled the tabernacle?
likely_questions.purpose: The text highlights the overwhelming presence and ordered access; later priestly and Hebrews material develops the issue.

likely_questions.question: Which Old Testament laws apply to Christians?
likely_questions.purpose: Begin with covenant context, then follow New Testament reaffirmation, fulfillment, transformation, or discontinuity; avoid one mechanical rule.

family.title: Rescue to Presence
family.parent_intro: This study connects the law and tabernacle to the Exodus rather than treating them as disconnected religious rules.

flow.instructions: Use the opening prompt to connect the lesson to ordinary family life.
Name what God had done, what Israel was called to be, and why the sanctuary was built.
Arrange Rescue, Vocation, Boundary, and Presence and explain each link.
Choose the weekly action, then pray together.

questions: Why does rescue come before law?
How can God be near while access is still ordered?

interactive.title: Four-Stage Covenant Map
interactive.instructions: Connect Rescue, Vocation, Boundary, and Presence with passage evidence.

family.weekly_action: Before applying one Bible command this week, ask: Who was addressed, under which covenant, and how does the New Testament use it?
family.prayer: Holy God, thank You for rescue and presence. Teach us reverence, obedience, and careful reading.
family.parent_note: Do not use holiness or obedience language to justify fear-based control. Questions about application are part of faithful study.

accessibility.reading_level: Teen discussion with technical terms defined and claims tested against context.
accessibility.plain_language_rule: Use precise language; define specialist terms and separate evidence from conclusion.
neurodiversity_supports: Allow written rather than spoken responses.
sensory_notes: No required role-play, public disclosure, or competitive performance.
non_reader_support: Provide concise claim cards or summaries without replacing the biblical text.

do_not_ask: Do not require disclosure of rule-breaking or religious fear.
Do not use holy presence language to justify coercive leadership.
safeguarding.teacher_response: Distinguish biblical reverence from manipulative fear. Provide private support pathways for students reporting spiritual coercion or abuse.
